entries.f3c15f02e49597e57b15e01dabf137f4cfa66fba: <div sID="gen20500" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Mic.7" sID="Mic.7"/> <div eID="gen20500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20501" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20502" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The prophet, in the name of the church, sadly laments the woeful decay of religion in the age wherein he lived, and the deluge of impiety and immorality which overwhelmed the nation, which levelled the differences, and bore down the fences, of all that is just and sacred, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.1-Mic.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The prophet, for the sake of the church, prescribes comforts, which may be of use at such a time, and gives counsel what to do. 1. They must have an eye to God, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.7">ver. 7</reference>. 2. They must courageously bear up against the insolences of the enemy, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8-Mic.7.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 3. They must patiently lie down under the rebukes of their God, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">ver. 9</reference>. 4. They must expect no other than that the trouble would continue long, and must endeavour to make the best of it, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.11-Mic.7.13">ver. 11-13</reference>. 5. They must encourage themselves with God's promises, in answer to the prophet's prayers, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14-Mic.7.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. 6. They must foresee the fall of their enemies, that now triumphed over them, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.16-Mic.7.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. 7. They must themselves triumph in the mercy and grace of God, and his faithfulness to his covenant (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18-Mic.7.20">ver. 18-20</reference>), and with that comfortable word the prophecy concludes.
entries.329f13f33b61eef4a58b45cb509f8842a12e4c60: <div eID="gen20502" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20501" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 700.)</title> <div sID="gen20503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grape-gleanings of the vintage: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no cluster to eat: my soul desired the first-ripe fruit. <hi type="super">2</hi> The good <hi type="italic">man</hi> is perished out of the earth: and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net. <hi type="super">3</hi> That they may do evil with both hands earnestly, the prince asketh, and the judge <hi type="italic">asketh</hi> for a reward; and the great <hi type="italic">man,</hi> he uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up. <hi type="super">4</hi> The best of them <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a brier: the most upright <hi type="italic">is sharper</hi> than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity. <hi type="super">5</hi> Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide: keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies <hi type="italic">are</hi> the men of his own house. <div eID="gen20503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20504" type="x-p"/> This is such a description of bad times as, some think, could scarcely agree to the times of Hezekiah, when this prophet prophesied; and therefore they rather take it as a prediction of what should be in the reign of Manasseh. But we may rather suppose it to be in the reign of Ahaz (and in that reign he prophesied, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>) or in the beginning of Hezekiah's time, before the reformation he was instrumental in; nay, in the best of his days, and when he had done his best to purge out corruptions, still there was much amiss. The prophet cries out, <hi type="italic">Woe is me!</hi> He bemoans himself that his lot was cast in such a degenerate age, and thinks it his great unhappiness that he lived among a people that were ripening apace for a ruin which many a good man would unavoidably be involved in. Thus David cries out, <hi type="italic">Woe is me that I sojourn in Mesech!</hi> He laments, 1. That there were so few good people to be found, even among those that were God's people; and this was their reproach: <hi type="italic">The good man has perished out of the earth,</hi> or <hi type="italic">out of the land,</hi> the land of Canaan; it was a <hi type="italic">good land,</hi> and <hi type="italic">a land of uprightness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa. xxvi. 10</reference>), but there were few good men in it, none upright among them, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">v. 2</reference>. The <hi type="italic">good man</hi> is a <hi type="italic">godly man</hi> and a <hi type="italic">merciful man;</hi> the word signifies both. Those are completely good men that are devout towards God and compassionate and beneficent towards men, that love mercy and walk with God. "These have perished; those few honest men that some time ago enriched and adorned our country are now dead and gone, and there are none risen up <hi type="italic">in their stead</hi> that tread in their steps; honesty is banished, and there is no such thing as a good man to be met with. Those that were of religious education have degenerated, and become as bad as the worst; <hi type="italic">the godly man ceases,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1">Ps. xii. 1</reference>. This is illustrated by a comparison (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.1">v. 1</reference>): they were <hi type="italic">as when they have gathered the summer fruits;</hi> it was as hard a thing to find a good man as to find any of the summer-fruits (which were the choicest and best, and therefore must carefully be gathered in) when the harvest is over. The prophet is ready to say, as Elijah in his time (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1 Kings xix. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">I, even I only, am left.</hi> Good men, who used to hang in clusters, are now as the <hi type="italic">grape-gleanings of the vintage,</hi> here and there a berry, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Isa. xvii. 6</reference>. You can find no societies of them as bunches of grapes, but those that are are single persons: <hi type="italic">There is no cluster to eat;</hi> and the best and fullest grapes are those that grow in large clusters. Some think that this intimates not only that good people were few, but that those few who remained, who went for good people, were good for little, like the small withered grapes, the refuse that were left behind, not only by the gatherer, but by the gleaner. When the prophet observed this universal degeneracy it made him <hi type="italic">desire the first-ripe fruit;</hi> he wished to see such worthy good men as were in the former ages, were the ornaments of the primitive times, and as far excelled the best of all the present age as the first and full-ripe fruits do those of the latter growth, that never come to maturity. When we read and hear of the wisdom and zeal, the strictness and conscientiousness, the devotion and charity, of the professors of religion in former ages, and see the reverse of this in those of the present age, we cannot but sit down, and wish, with a sigh, <hi type="italic">O for primitive Christianity again!</hi> Where are the plainness and integrity of those that went before us? Where are the Israelites indeed, without guile? Our souls desire them, but in vain. The golden age is gone, and past recall; we must make the best of what is, for we are not likely to see such times as have been. 2. That there were so many wicked mischievous people among them, not only none that did any good, but multitudes that did all the hurt they could: "<hi type="italic">They all lie in wait for blood,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hunt every man his brother.</hi> To get wealth to themselves, they care not what wrong, what hurt, they do to their neighbours and nearest relations. They act as if mankind were in a state of war, and force were the only right. They are as beasts of prey to their neighbours, for <hi type="italic">they all lie in wait for blood</hi> as lions for their prey; they thirst after it, make nothing of taking away any man's life or livelihood to serve a turn for themselves, and lie in wait for an opportunity to do it. Their neighbours are as beasts of prey to them, for they <hi type="italic">hunt every man his brother with a net;</hi> they persecute them as noxious creatures, fit to be taken and destroyed, though they are innocent excellent ones." We say of him that is outlawed, <hi type="italic">Caput gerit lupinum—He is to be hunted as a wolf.</hi> "Or they hunt them as men do the game, to feast upon it; they have a thousand cursed arts of ensnaring men to their ruin, so that they may but get by it. Thus <hi type="italic">they do mischief with both hands earnestly;</hi> their hearts desire it, their heads contrive it, and then <hi type="italic">both hands</hi> are ready to put it in execution." Note, The more eager and intent men are upon any sinful pursuit, and the more pains they take in it, the more provoking it is. 3. That the magistrates, who by their office ought to have been the patrons and protectors of right, were the practicers and promoters of wrong: <hi type="italic">That they may do evil with both hands earnestly,</hi> to excite and animate themselves in it, <hi type="italic">the prince asketh, and the judge asketh, for a reward,</hi> for a bribe, with which they well be hired to exert all their power for the supporting and carrying on of any wicked design <hi type="italic">with both hands. They do evil with both hands well</hi> (so some read it); they do evil with a great deal of art and dexterity; they praise themselves for doing it so well. Others read it thus: <hi type="italic">To do evil they have both hands</hi> (they catch at an opportunity of doing mischief), <hi type="italic">but to do good the prince and the judge ask for a reward;</hi> if they do any good offices they are mercenary in them, and must be paid for them. The great man, who has wealth and power to do good, is not ashamed to utter his mischievous desire in conjunction with the prince and the judge, who are ready to support him and stand by him in it. <hi type="italic">So they wrap it up;</hi> they perplex the matter, involve it, and make it intricate (so some understand it), that they may lose equity in a mist, and so make the cause turn which way they please. It is ill with a people when their princes, and judges, and great men are in a confederacy to pervert justice. And it is a sad character that is given of them (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.4">v. 4</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the best of them is as a brier, and the most upright is sharper than a thorn-hedge;</hi> it is a dangerous thing to have any thing to do with them; <hi type="italic">he that touches them must be fenced with iron</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6-2Sam.23.7">2 Sam. xxiii. 6, 7</reference>), he shall be sure to be scratched, to have his clothes torn, and his eyes almost pulled out. And, if this be the character of the best and most upright, what are the worst? And, when things have come to this pass, <hi type="italic">the day of thy watchmen comes,</hi> that is, as it follows, <hi type="italic">the day of thy visitation,</hi> when God will reckon with thee for all this wickedness, which is called <hi type="italic">the day of the watchmen,</hi> because their prophets, whom God set as watchmen over them, had often warned them of that day. When all flesh have corrupted their way, even the best and the most upright, what can be expected but a day of visitation, a deluge of judgments, as that which drowned the old world when <hi type="italic">the earth was filled with violence?</hi> 4. That there was no faith in man; people had grown so universally treacherous that one knew not whom to repose any confidence in, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.5">v. 5</reference>. "Those that have any sense of honour, or spark of virtue, remaining in them, have a firm regard to the laws of friendship; they would not discover what passed in private conversation, nor divulge secrets, to the prejudice of a friend. But those things are now made a jest of; you will not meet with a friend that you dare trust, whose word you dare take, or who will have any tenderness or concern for you; so that wise men shall give it and take it for a rule, <hi type="italic">trust you not in a friend,</hi> for you will find him false, you can trust him no further than you can see him; and even him that passes for an honest man you will find to be so only with good looking to. Nay, as for him that undertakes to be <hi type="italic">your guide,</hi> to lead you into any business which he professes to understand better than you, you cannot <hi type="italic">put a confidence</hi> in him, for he will be sure to mislead you if he can get any thing by it." Some by a guide understand a husband, who is called <hi type="italic">the guide of thy youth;</hi> and that agrees well enough with what follows, "<hi type="italic">Keep the doors of thy lips from her that lieth in thy bosom,</hi> from thy own wife; take heed what thou sayest before her, lest she betray thee, as Delilah did Samson, lest she be the <hi type="italic">bird of the air</hi> that <hi type="italic">carries the voice</hi> of that which thou sayest <hi type="italic">in thy bed-chamber,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">Eccl. x. 20</reference>. It is an evil time indeed when the prudent are obliged even thus far to keep silence. 5. That children were abusive to their parents, and men had no comfort, no satisfaction, in their own families and their nearest relations, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.6">v. 6</reference>. The times are bad indeed when <hi type="italic">the son dishonours his father,</hi> gives him bad language, exposes him, threatens him, and studies to do him a mischief, <hi type="italic">when the daughter rises up</hi> in rebellion against her own mother, having no sense of duty, or natural affection; and no marvel that then the <hi type="italic">daughter-in-law</hi> quarrels with her <hi type="italic">mother-in-law,</hi> and is vexatious to her. Either they cannot agree about their property and interest, or their humours and passions clash, or from a spirit of bigotry and persecution, <hi type="italic">the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.4">Matt. x. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.16">Luke xxi. 16</reference>. It is sad when a man's betrayers and worst enemies are the men of his own house, his own children and servants, that should be his guard and his best friends. Note, The contempt and violation of the laws of domestic duties are a sad symptom of a universal corruption of manners. Those are never likely to come to good that are undutiful to their parents, and study to be provoking to them and cross them.
entries.2d3d7f0bde9481a691d0677cacc5db4cdd84e601: <div eID="gen20504" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Seeking Comfort in God; The Sins of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 700.)</title> <div sID="gen20505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore I will look unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me. <hi type="super">8</hi> Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a light unto me. <hi type="super">9</hi> I will bear the indignation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I shall behold his righteousness. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then <hi type="italic">she that is</hi> mine enemy shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and shame shall cover her which said unto me, Where is the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God? mine eyes shall behold her: now shall she be trodden down as the mire of the streets.   11 <hi type="italic">In</hi> the day that thy walls are to be built, <hi type="italic">in</hi> that day shall the decree be far removed. <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">In</hi> that day <hi type="italic">also</hi> he shall come even to thee from Assyria, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the fortified cities, and from the fortress even to the river, and from sea to sea, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> mountain to mountain. <hi type="super">13</hi> Notwithstanding the land shall be desolate because of them that dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings. <div eID="gen20505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20506" type="x-p"/> The prophet, having sadly complained of the wickedness of the times he lived in, here fastens upon some considerations for the comfort of himself and his friends, in reference thereunto. The case is bad, but it is not desperate. <hi type="italic">Yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing.</hi> <div eID="gen20506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20507" type="x-p"/> I. "Though God be now displeased he shall be reconciled to us, and then all will be well, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">9</reference>. We are now under <hi type="italic">the indignation of the Lord;</hi> God is angry with us, and justly, because <hi type="italic">we have sinned against him.</hi>" Note, It is our sin against God that provokes his indignation against us; and we must see it, and own it, whenever we are under divine rebukes, that we may justify God, and may study to answer his end in afflicting us, by repenting of sin and breaking off from it. Now, at such a time, 1. We must have recourse to God under our troubles (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore I will look unto the Lord.</hi> When a child of God has ever so much occasion to cry, <hi type="italic">Woe is me</hi> (as the prophet here, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.1">v. 1</reference>), yet it may be a comfort to him that he has a God to look to, a God to come to, to fly to, in whom he may rejoice and have satisfaction. All may look bright above him when all looks black and dark about him. The prophet had been complaining that there was no comfort to be had, no confidence to be put, in friends and relations on earth, and this drives him to his God: <hi type="italic">Therefore I will look unto the Lord.</hi> The less reason we have to delight in any creature the more reason we have to delight in God. If princes are not to be trusted, we may say, <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that has</hi> the God of Jacob for his help, and <hi type="italic">happy am I,</hi> even in the midst of my present woes, if he be my help. If men be false, this is our comfort, that God is faithful; if relations be unkind, he is and will be gracious. Let us therefore look above and beyond them, and overlook our disappointment in them, and look unto the Lord. 2. We must submit to the will of God in our troubles: "<hi type="italic">I will bear the indignation of the Lord,</hi> will bear it patiently, without murmuring and repining, <hi type="italic">because I have sinned against him.</hi>" Note, Those that are truly penitent for sin will see a great deal of reason to be patient under affliction. <hi type="italic">Wherefore should a man complain for the punishment of his sin?</hi> When we complain to God of the badness of the times we ought to complain against ourselves for the badness of our own hearts. 3. We must depend upon God to work deliverance for us, and put a good issue to our troubles in due time; we must not only look to him, but look for him: "I will <hi type="italic">wait for the God of my salvation,</hi> and for his gracious returns to me." In our greatest distresses we shall see no reason to despair of salvation if by faith we eye God as the <hi type="italic">God of our salvation,</hi> who is able to save the weakest upon their humble petition, and willing to save the worst upon their true repentance. And, if we depend on God as the God of our salvation, we must wait for him, and for his salvation, in his own way and his own time. Let us now see what the church is here taught to expect and promise herself from God, even when things are brought to the last extremity. (1.) <hi type="italic">My God will hear me;</hi> if the Lord be our God, he will hear our prayers, and grant an answer of peace to them. (2.) "<hi type="italic">When I fall,</hi> and am in danger of being dashed in pieces by the fall, yet <hi type="italic">I shall arise,</hi> and recover myself again. <hi type="italic">I fall,</hi> but am not <hi type="italic">utterly cast down,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">Ps. xxxvii. 24</reference>. (3.) "<hi type="italic">When I sit in darkness,</hi> desolate and disconsolate, melancholy and perplexed, and not knowing what to do, nor which way to look for relief, yet then <hi type="italic">the Lord shall be a light to me,</hi> to comfort and revive me, to instruct and teach me, to direct and guide me, as a light to my eyes, a light to my feet, a light <hi type="italic">in a dark place.</hi>" (4.) <hi type="italic">He will plead my cause, and execute judgment for me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">v. 9</reference>. If we heartily espouse the cause of God, the just but injured cause of religion and virtue, and make it our cause, we may hope he will own our cause, and plead it. The church's cause, though it seem for a time to go against her, will at length be pleaded with jealousy, and judgment not only given against, but executed upon, the enemies of it. (5.) "He <hi type="italic">will bring me forth to the light,</hi> make me shine eminently out of obscurity, and become conspicuous, will make my righteousness shine evidently from under the dark cloud of calumny, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.6">Ps. xxxvii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Isa. lviii. 10</reference>. The morning of comfort shall shine forth out of the long and dark night of trouble." (6.) "<hi type="italic">I shall behold his righteousness;</hi> I shall see the equity of his proceedings concerning me and the performance of his promises to me." <div eID="gen20507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20508" type="x-p"/> II. Though enemies triumph and insult, they shall be silenced and put to shame, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.10">10</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen20508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20509" type="x-p"/> 1. How proudly the enemies of God's people trample upon them in their distress. They said, <hi type="italic">Where is the Lord their God?</hi> As if because they were afflicted God had forsaken them, and they knew not where to find him with their prayers, and he knew not how to help them with his favours. This David's enemies said to him, and it was a sword in his bones, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Ps. xlii. 10</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Ps. cxv. 2</reference>. Thus, in reproaching Israel as an abandoned people, they reflected on the God of Israel as an unkind unfaithful God. <div eID="gen20509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20510" type="x-p"/> 2. How comfortably the people of God by faith bear up themselves under these insults (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Rejoice not against me, O my enemy!</hi> I am now down, but shall not be always so, and when my God appears for me then <hi type="italic">she that is my enemy shall see it, and be ashamed</hi>" (not only being disappointed in her expectations of the church's utter ruin, but having the same cup of trembling put into her hand), "then <hi type="italic">my eyes shall behold her</hi> in the same deplorable condition that I am now in; <hi type="italic">now shall she be trodden down.</hi>" Note, The deliverance of the church will be the confusion of her enemies; and their shame shall be double, when, as they have trampled upon God's people, so they shall themselves be trampled upon. <div eID="gen20510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20511" type="x-p"/> III. Though the land continue a great while desolate, yet it shall at length be replenished again, when the time, even the set time, of its deliverance comes. 1. Its salvation shall not come <hi type="italic">till after it has been desolate;</hi> so the margin reads it, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.13">v. 13</reference>. God has a controversy with the land, and it must lie long under his rebukes, <hi type="italic">because of those that dwell therein;</hi> it is their iniquity that makes their land desolate (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Ps. cvii. 34</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">for the fruit of their doings,</hi> their evil doings which they have been themselves guilty of, and the evil fruit of them, the sins of others, which they have been accessory to by their bad influence and example. For this they must expect to smart a great while; for the world shall know that God hates sin even in his own people. 2. When it does come it shall be a complete salvation; and it seems to refer to their deliverance out of Babylon by Cyrus, which Isaiah about this time prophesied of, as a type of our redemption by Christ. (1.) <hi type="italic">The decree shall be far removed.</hi> God's decree concerning their captivity, and Nebuchadnezzar's decree concerning the perpetuity of it, his resolution never to release them, "these shall be set aside and revoked, and you shall hear no more of them; they shall no more lie as a yoke upon thy neck." (2.) Jerusalem and the cities of Judah shall be again reared: Then <hi type="italic">thy walls shall be built,</hi> walls for habitation, walls for defence, house-walls, town-walls, temple-walls; it is in order to these that the decree is repealed, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa. xliv. 28</reference>. Though Zion's walls may lie long in ruins, there will come a day when they shall be repaired. (3.) All that belong to the land of Israel, whithersoever dispersed, and howsoever distressed, far and wide over the face of the whole earth, shall come flocking to it again (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall come even to thee,</hi> having liberty to return and a heart to return, from Assyria, whither the ten tribes were carried away, though it lay remote, and <hi type="italic">from the fortified cities,</hi> and <hi type="italic">from the fortress,</hi> those strongholds in which they thought they had them fast; for when God's time comes, though Pharaoh will not <hi type="italic">let the people go,</hi> God will fetch them out with a high hand. They shall come from all the remote parts, <hi type="italic">from sea to sea</hi> and <hi type="italic">from mountain to mountain,</hi> not turning back for fear of your discouragements, but they shall go from strength to strength till they come to Zion. Thus in the great day of redemption <hi type="italic">God will gather his elect from the four winds.</hi>
entries.49b8f02c3a16f533b37c1628482010374f3130d5: <div eID="gen20511" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouraging Prospects; Encouraging Promises. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 700.)</title> <div sID="gen20512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily <hi type="italic">in</hi> the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed <hi type="italic">in</hi> Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. <hi type="super">15</hi> According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous <hi type="italic">things.</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might: they shall lay <hi type="italic">their</hi> hand upon <hi type="italic">their</hi> mouth, their ears shall be deaf. <hi type="super">17</hi> They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth: they shall be afraid of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, and shall fear because of thee. <hi type="super">18</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth <hi type="italic">in</hi> mercy. <hi type="super">19</hi> He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old. <div eID="gen20512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20513" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The prophet's prayer to God to take care of his own people, and of their cause and interest, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">v. 14</reference>. When God is about to deliver his people he stirs up their friends to pray for them, and pours out <hi type="italic">a spirit of grace and supplication,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>. And when we see God coming towards us in ways of mercy, we must go forth to meet him by prayer. It is a prophetic prayer, which amounts to a promise of the good prayed for; what God directed his prophet to ask no doubt he designed to give. Now, 1. The people of Israel are here called the <hi type="italic">flock of God's heritage,</hi> for they are the sheep of his hand, the sheep of his pasture, his little flock in the world; and they are his heritage, his portion in the world. <hi type="italic">Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.</hi> 2. This flock <hi type="italic">dwells solitarily in the wood,</hi> or <hi type="italic">forest, in the midst of Carmel,</hi> a high mountain. Israel was a peculiar people, <hi type="italic">that dwelt alone, and was not reckoned among the nations,</hi> like a flock of sheep in a wood. They were now a desolate people (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.13">v. 13</reference>), were in the land of their captivity as sheep in a forest, in danger of being lost and made a prey of to the beasts of the forest. They are <hi type="italic">scattered upon the mountains as sheep having no shepherd.</hi> 3. He prays that God would <hi type="italic">feed them there with his rod,</hi> that is, that he would take care of them in their captivity, would protect them, and provide for them, and do the part of a good shepherd to them: "Let <hi type="italic">thy rod and staff comfort</hi> them, even in that darksome valley; and even there let them want nothing that is good for them. Let them be governed by thy rod, not the rod of their enemies, for they are thy people." 4. He prays that God would in due time bring them back to feed in the plains of Bashan and Gilead, and no longer to be fed in the woods and mountains. <hi type="italic">Let them feed</hi> in their own country again, <hi type="italic">as in the days of old.</hi> Some apply this spiritually, and make it either the prophet's prayer to Christ or his Father's charge to him, to take care of his church, as the great Shepherd of the sheep, and to go in and out before them while they are here in this world as in a wood, that they may find pasture as in Carmel, as in Bashan and Gilead. <div eID="gen20513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20514" type="x-p"/> II. God's promise, in answer to this prayer; and we may well take God's promises as real answers to the prayers of faith, and embrace them accordingly, for with him saying and doing are not two things. The prophet prayed that God would feed them, and do kind things for them; but God answers that he <hi type="italic">will show them marvellous things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.15">v. 15</reference>), will do for them more than they are able to ask or think, will out-do their hopes and expectations; he will <hi type="italic">show them his marvellous lovingkindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.7">Ps. xvii. 7</reference>. 1. He will do that for them which shall be the repetition of the wonders and miracles of former ages—<hi type="italic">according to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt.</hi> Their deliverance out of Babylon shall be a work of wonder and grace not inferior to their deliverance out of Egypt, nay, it shall eclipse the lustre of that (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.14-Jer.16.15">Jer. xvi. 14, 15</reference>), much more shall the work of redemption by Christ. Note, God's former favours to his church are patterns of future favours, and shall again be copied out as there is occasion. 2. He will do that for them which shall be matter of wonder and amazement to the present age, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.16-Mic.7.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. The <hi type="italic">nations about</hi> shall take notice of it, and it shall be said <hi type="italic">among the heathen, The Lord has done great things for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.126.2">Ps. cxxvi. 2</reference>. The impression which the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon shall make upon the neighbouring nations shall be very much for the honour both of God and his church. (1.) Those that had insulted over the people of God in their distress, and gloried that when they had them down they would keep them down, <hi type="italic">shall be confounded,</hi> when they see them thus surprisingly rising up; they shall be <hi type="italic">confounded at all the might</hi> with which the captives shall now exert themselves, whom they thought for ever disabled. They shall now <hi type="italic">lay their hands upon their mouths,</hi> as being ashamed of what they have said, and not able to say more, by way of triumph over Israel. Nay, <hi type="italic">their ears shall be deaf</hi> too, so much shall they be ashamed at the wonderful deliverance; they shall stop their ears, as being not willing to hear any more of God's wonders wrought for that people, whom they had so despised and insulted over. (2.) Those that had impudently confronted God himself shall now be struck with a fear of him, and thereby brought, in profession at least, to submit to him (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall lick the dust like a serpent,</hi> they shall be so mortified, as if they were sentenced to the same curse the serpent was laid under (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14">Gen. iii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat.</hi> They shall be brought to the lowest abasements imaginable, and shall be so dispirited that they shall tamely submit to them. <hi type="italic">His enemies shall lick the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.9">Ps. lxxii. 9</reference>. Nay, they shall <hi type="italic">lick the dust</hi> of the church's feet, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Isa. xlix. 23</reference>. Proud oppressors shall now be made sensible how mean, how little, they are, before the great God, and they shall with trembling and the lowest submission <hi type="italic">move out of the holes</hi> into which they had crept (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa. ii. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">like worms of the earth</hi> as they are, being ashamed and afraid to <hi type="italic">show their heads;</hi> so low shall they be brought, and such abjects shall they be, when they are abased. When God did wonders for his church <hi type="italic">many of the people of the land became Jews,</hi> because <hi type="italic">the fear of the Jews,</hi> and of their God, <hi type="italic">fell upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Esth. viii. 17</reference>. So it is promised here: <hi type="italic">They shall be afraid of the Lord our God, and shall fear because of thee, O Israel!</hi> Forced submissions are often but feigned submissions; yet they redound to the glory of God and the church, though not to the benefit of the dissemblers themselves. <div eID="gen20514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20515" type="x-p"/> III. The prophet's thankful acknowledgment of God's mercy, in the name of the church, with a believing dependence upon his promise, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18-Mic.7.20">v. 18-20</reference>. We are here taught, <div eID="gen20515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20516" type="x-p"/> 1. To give to God the glory of his pardoning mercy, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">v. 18</reference>. God having promised to bring back the captivity of his people, the prophet, on that occasion, admires pardoning mercy, as that which was at the bottom of it. As it was their sin that brought them into bondage, so it was God's pardoning their sin that brought them our of it; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.2 Isa.33.24 Isa.38.17 Isa.60.1-Isa.60.2">Ps. lxxxv. 1, 2, and Isa. xxxiii. 24; xxxviii. 17; lx. 1, 2</reference>. The pardon of sin is the foundation of all other covenant-mercies, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.12">Heb. viii. 12</reference>. This the prophet stands amazed at, while the surrounding nations stood amazed only at those deliverances which were but the fruits of this. Note, (1.) God's people, who are the <hi type="italic">remnant of his heritage,</hi> stand charged with many transgressions; being but a remnant, a very few, one would hope they should all be very good, but they are not so; God's children have their spots, and often offend their Father. (2.) The gracious God is ready to pass by and pardon the iniquity and transgression of his people, upon their repentance and return to him. God's people are a pardoned people, and to this they owe their all. When God pardons sin, he passes it by, does not punish it as justly he might, nor deal with the sinner according to the desert of it. (3.) Though God may for a time lay his own people under the tokens of his displeasure, yet he will not <hi type="italic">retain his anger for ever,</hi> but <hi type="italic">though he cause grief he will have compassion;</hi> he is not implacable; yet against those that are not of the remnant of his heritage, that are unpardoned, he will keep his anger for ever. (4.) The reasons why God pardons sin, and keeps not his anger for ever, are all taken from within himself; it is <hi type="italic">because he delights in mercy,</hi> and the salvation of sinners is what he has pleasure in, not their death and damnation. (5.) The glory of God in forgiving sin is, as in other things, matchless, and without compare. There is <hi type="italic">no God like unto him</hi> for this; no magistrate, no common person, forgives as God does. In this his thoughts and ways are infinitely above ours; in this he is <hi type="italic">God, and not man.</hi> (6.) All those that have experienced pardoning mercy cannot but admire that mercy; it is what we have reason to stand amazed at, if we know what it is. Has God forgiven us our transgressions? We may well say, <hi type="italic">Who is a God like unto thee?</hi> Our holy wonder at pardoning mercy will be a good evidence of our interest in it. <div eID="gen20516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20517" type="x-p"/> 2. To take to ourselves the comfort of that mercy and all the grace and truth that go along with it. God's people here, as they look back with thankfulness upon God's pardoning their sins, so they look forward with assurance upon what he would yet further do for them. His mercy <hi type="italic">endures for ever,</hi> and therefore as he has <hi type="italic">shown mercy</hi> so he will, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19-Mic.7.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. (1.) He will renew his favours to us: <hi type="italic">He will turn again; he will have compassion;</hi> that is, he will again have compassion upon us as formerly he had; his compassions shall be <hi type="italic">new every morning;</hi> he seemed to be departing from us in anger, but he will turn again and pity us. He will turn us to himself, and then will <hi type="italic">turn to us, and have mercy upon us.</hi> (2.) He will renew us, to prepare and qualify us for his favour: <hi type="italic">He will subdue our iniquities;</hi> when he takes away the guilt of sin, that it may not damn us, he will break the power of sin, that it may not have dominion over us, that we may not fear sin, nor be led captive by it. Sin is an enemy that fights against us, a tyrant that oppresses us; nothing less than almighty grace can subdue it, so great is its power in fallen man and so long has it kept possession. But, if God forgive the sin that has been committed by us, he will subdue the sin that dwells in us, and in that there is none like him in forgiving; and all those whose sins are pardoned earnestly desire and hope; to have their corruptions mortified and their iniquities subdued, and please themselves with the hopes of it. If we be left to ourselves, our iniquities will be too hard for us; but God's grace, we trust, shall be sufficient for us to subdue them, so that they shall not rule us, and then they shall not ruin us. (3.) He will confirm this good work, and effectually provide that his act of grace shall never be repealed: <hi type="italic">Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depth of the sea,</hi> as when he brought them out of Egypt (to which he has an eye in the promises here, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.15">v. 15</reference>) he subdued Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and cast them into the depth of the sea. It intimates that when God forgives sin he <hi type="italic">remembers it no more,</hi> and takes care that it shall never be remembered more against the sinner. <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.22">Ezek. xviii. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">His transgressions shall not be mentioned unto him;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">blotted out as a cloud</hi> which never appears more. He casts them into the sea, not near the shore-side, where they may appear again next low water, but into <hi type="italic">the depth of the sea,</hi> never to rise again. <hi type="italic">All their sins</hi> shall be cast there without exception, for when God forgives sin he forgives all. (4.) He will perfect that which concerns us, and with this good work will do all that for us which our case requires and which he has promised (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then wilt thou perform thy truth to Jacob and thy mercy to Abraham.</hi> It is in pursuance of the covenant that our sins are pardoned and our lusts mortified; from that spring all these streams flow, and with these he shall <hi type="italic">freely give us all things.</hi> The promise is said to be <hi type="italic">mercy to Abraham,</hi> because, as made to him first, it was mere mercy, preventing mercy, considering what state it found him in. But it was <hi type="italic">truth to Jacob,</hi> because the faithfulness of God was engaged to make good to him and his seed, as heirs to Abraham, all that was graciously promised to Abraham. See here, [1.] With what solemnity the covenant of grace is ratified to us; it was not only spoken, written, and sealed, but which is the highest confirmation, it was <hi type="italic">sworn to our fathers;</hi> nor is it a modern project, but is confirmed by antiquity too; it was sworn <hi type="italic">from the days of old;</hi> it is an ancient charter. [2.] With what satisfaction it may be applied and relied upon by us; we may say with the highest assurance, <hi type="italic">Thou wilt perform the truth and mercy;</hi> not one iota or tittle of it shall fall to the ground. Faithful is he that has promised, who also will do it.  <chapter eID="Mic.7"/> <div eID="gen20517" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20385" osisID="Mic" type="book"/>

entries.36d663343d769c819d1af386b44a8be1e219739b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12799"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.7.1-Mic.7.20">Mi 7:1-20</reference>. The Universality of the Corruption; the Chosen Remnant, Driven from Every Human Confidence, Turns to God; Triumphs by Faith over Her Enemies; Is Comforted by God's Promises in Answer to Prayer, and by the Confusion of Her Enemies, and So Breaks Forth into Praises of God's Character.</title> <div sID="gen23767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12799"/><hi type="bold">1. I am as when, &c.--</hi>It is the same with me as with one seeking fruits after the harvest, grapes after the vintage. "There is not a cluster" to be found: no "first-ripe fruit" (or "early fig"; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Is 28:4</reference>) which "my soul desireth" [Maurer]. So I look in vain for any good men left (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mi 7:2</reference>). <div eID="gen23767" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bda7be80b5cab3f7ebd4ab38114060f041f4c47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12800"/><div sID="gen23768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12800"/>2. The Hebrew expresses "one merciful and good in relation to man," rather than to God.<div eID="gen23768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is perished out of the earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.12.1">Psa 12:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23769" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd78a9f8d864cead9dee82b837f138125e3df63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12801"/><div sID="gen23770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12801"/><hi type="bold">3. That they may do evil with both hands earnestly--</hi>literally, "Their hands are for evil that they may do it well" (that is, cleverly and successfully).<div eID="gen23770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the great man, he--</hi>emphatic repetition. As for the great man, he no sooner has expressed his bad desire (literally, the "mischief" or "lust of his soul"), than the venal judges are ready to wrest the decision of the case according to his wish.<div eID="gen23771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so they wrap it up--</hi>The Hebrew is used of intertwining cords together. The "threefold cord is not quickly broken" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">Ec 4:12</reference>); here the "prince," the "judge," and the "great man" are the three in guilty complicity. "They wrap it up," namely, they conspire to carry out the great man's desire at the sacrifice of justice. <div eID="gen23772" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbad8dfc757122184b45364dfe423129c1f560f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12802"/><div sID="gen23773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12802"/><hi type="bold">4. as a brier--</hi>or thorn; pricking with injury all who come in contact with them (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.13">Is 55:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.6">Eze 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of thy watchmen--</hi>the day foretold by thy (true) prophets, as the time of "thy visitation" in wrath [Grotius]. Or, "the day of thy false prophets being punished"; they are specially threatened as being not only blind themselves, but leading others blindfold [Calvin].<div eID="gen23774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>at the time foretold, "at that time"; the prophet transporting himself into it.<div eID="gen23775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perplexity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.22.5">Is 22:5</reference>). They shall not know whither to turn. <div eID="gen23776" type="x-p"/>
entries.db80eeca6216c224948e7f7c083cbbb9c72f40c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12803"/><div sID="gen23777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12803"/><hi type="bold">5. Trust ye not in a friend--</hi>Faith is kept nowhere: all to a man are treacherous (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.2-Jer.9.6">Jr 9:2-6</reference>). When justice is perverted by the great, faith nowhere is safe. So, in gospel times of persecution, "a man's foes are they of his own household" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.35">Mt 10:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.53">Lu 12:53</reference>).<div eID="gen23777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">guide--</hi>a counsellor [Calvin] able to help and advise (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.8">Psa 118:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">146:3</reference>). The head of your family, to whom all the members of the family would naturally repair in emergencies. Similarly the Hebrew is translated in <reference osisRef="Josh.22.14">Jos 22:14</reference> and "chief friends" in <reference osisRef="Prov.16.28">Pr 16:28</reference> [Grotius].<div eID="gen23778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her that lieth in thy bosom--</hi>thy wife (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">De 13:6</reference>). <div eID="gen23779" type="x-p"/>
entries.509b304f4ccad05ccabe7cb042519f396edfe2fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12804"/><div sID="gen23780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12804"/><hi type="bold">6. son dishonoureth the father--</hi>The state of unnatural lawlessness in all relations of life is here described which is to characterize the last times, before Messiah comes to punish the ungodly and save Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.21.16">Lu 21:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.3">2Ti 3:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen23780" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e66527d30f5d5bb6748f704a8d2d3572a3beaa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12805"/><div sID="gen23781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12805"/><hi type="bold">7. Therefore I will look unto the Lord--</hi>as if no one else were before mine eyes. We must not only "look unto the Lord," but also "wait for Him." Having no hope from man (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.5">Mi 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.6">6</reference>), Micah speaks in the name of Israel, who herein, taught by chastisement (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.4">Mi 7:4</reference>) to feel her sin (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>), casts herself on the Lord as her only hope," in patient waiting (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">La 3:26</reference>). She did so under the Babylonian captivity; she shall do so again hereafter when the spirit of grace shall be poured on her (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.13">Zec 12:10-13</reference>). <div eID="gen23781" type="x-p"/>
entries.f44b68f5e230d1664b7ac14b29a20bdaf103136e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12806"/><div sID="gen23782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12806"/><hi type="bold">8. Rejoice not--</hi>at my fall.<div eID="gen23782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I fall, I shall arise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">Psa 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.16">Pr 24:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light--</hi>Israel reasons as her divine representative, Messiah, reasoned by faith in His hour of darkness and desertion (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Is 50:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">8, 10</reference>). Israel addresses Babylon, her triumphant foe (or Edom), as a female; the type of her last and worst foes (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">8</reference>). "Mine enemy," in Hebrew, is feminine. <div eID="gen23784" type="x-p"/>
entries.a02308050ca48e54467362f77f7d6af906fb9e3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12807"/><div sID="gen23785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12807"/><hi type="bold">9. bear--</hi>patiently.<div eID="gen23785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the indignation of the Lord--</hi>His punishment inflicted on me (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">La 3:39</reference>). The true penitent "accepts the punishment of his iniquity" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Le 26:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.43">43</reference>); they who murmur against God, do not yet know their guilt (<reference osisRef="Job.40.4">Job 40:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen23786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">execute judgment for me--</hi>against my foe. God's people plead guilty before God; but, in respect to their human foes, they are innocent and undeserving of their foes' injuries.<div eID="gen23787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring me forth to the light--</hi>to the temporal and spiritual redemption.<div eID="gen23788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I shall behold his righteousness--</hi>His gracious faithfulness to His promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.17">Psa 103:17</reference>). <div eID="gen23789" type="x-p"/>
entries.426476c3d0064bfb7337d7a319cf68dc333de118: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12808"/><div sID="gen23790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12808"/><hi type="bold">10. shame shall cover her--</hi>in seeing how utterly mistaken she was in supposing that I was utterly ruined.<div eID="gen23790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Where is ... thy God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">10</reference>). If He be "thy God," as thou sayest, let Him come now and deliver thee. So as to Israel's representative, Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.43">Mt 27:43</reference>).<div eID="gen23791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine eyes shall behold her--</hi>a just retribution in kind upon the foe who had said, "Let our eye look upon Zion." Zion shall behold her foe prostrate, not with the carnal joy of revenge, but with spiritual joy in God's vindicating His own righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Is 66:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.5-Rev.16.7">Re 16:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen23792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall she be trodden down--</hi>herself, who had trodden down me. <div eID="gen23793" type="x-p"/>
entries.2083163b1b504acdcfc3c931618643e5df0e4a95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12809"/><div sID="gen23794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12809"/><hi type="bold">11. thy walls ... be built--</hi>under Cyrus, after the seventy years' captivity; and again, hereafter, when the Jews shall be restored (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">Zec 12:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall the decree be far removed--</hi>namely, thy tyrannical decree or rule of Babylon shall be put away from thee, "the statutes that were not good" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.25">Eze 20:25</reference>) [Calvin]. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.16">Psa 102:13-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>. The Hebrew is against Maurer's translation, "the boundary of the city shall be far extended," so as to contain the people flocking into it from all nations (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.12">Mi 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.20">Is 49:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">54:2</reference>). <div eID="gen23795" type="x-p"/>
entries.068c0ba8ac674113bb185fb93d2182d697acb1ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12810"/><div sID="gen23796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12810"/><hi type="bold">12. In that day also--</hi>rather, an answer to the supposed question of Zion, When shall my walls be built? "The day (of thy walls being built) is the day when he (that is, many) shall come to thee from Assyria," &c. [Ludovicus De Dieu]. The Assyrians (including the Babylonians) who spoiled thee shall come.<div eID="gen23796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and from the fortified cities--</hi>rather, to suit the parallelism, "from Assyria even to Egypt." (Matzor may be so translated). So Assyria and Egypt are contrasted in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">Is 19:23</reference> [Maurer]. Calvin agrees with English Version, "from all fortified cities."<div eID="gen23797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the fortress even to the river--</hi>"from Egypt even to the river" Euphrates (answering in parallelism to "Assyria") [Maurer]. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Is 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23-Isa.19.25">19:23-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">Ho 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.10">Zec 10:10</reference>. <div eID="gen23798" type="x-p"/>
entries.654741d7408bf9ff804abced1ad5a7cf36f9c018: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12811"/><div sID="gen23799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12811"/>13. However glorious the prospect of restoration, the Jews are not to forget the visitation on their "land" which is to intervene for the "fruit of (evil caused by) their doings" (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Is 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.14">Jr 21:14</reference>). <div eID="gen23799" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff387c86ddfde244fa347015a2991d679bb10c83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12812"/><div sID="gen23800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12812"/><hi type="bold">14. Feed thy people--</hi>Prayer of the prophet, in the name of his people to God, which, as God fulfils believing prayer, is prophetical of what God would do. When God is about to deliver His people, He stirs up their friends to pray for them.<div eID="gen23800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Feed--</hi>including the idea of both pastoral rule and care over His people (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.4">Mi 5:4</reference>, Margin), regarded as a flock (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">100:3</reference>). Our calamity must be fatal to the nation, unless Thou of Thy unmerited grace, remembering Thy covenant with "Thine heritage" (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">De 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.6">7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">32:9</reference>), shalt restore us.<div eID="gen23801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy rod--</hi>the shepherd's rod, wherewith He directs the flock (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). No longer the rod of punishment (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.9">Mi 6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which dwell solitarily in the wood, in ... Carmel--</hi>Let Thy people who have been dwelling as it were in a solitude of woods (in the world, but not of it), scattered among various nations, dwell in Carmel, that is, where there are fruit-bearing lands and vineyards [Calvin]. Rather, "which are about to dwell (that is, that they may dwell) separate in the wood, in ... Carmel" [Maurer], which are to be no longer mingled with the heathen, but are to dwell as a distinct people in their own land. Micah has here Balaam's prophecy in view (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.6.5">Mi 6:5</reference>, where also Balaam is referred to). "Lo, the people shall dwell alone" (<reference osisRef="Num.23.9">Nu 23:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.28">De 33:28</reference>). To "feed in the wood in Carmel," is to feed in the rich pastures among its woods. To "sleep in the woods," is the image of most perfect security (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">Eze 34:25</reference>). So that the Jews' "security," as well as their distinct nationality, is here foretold. Also <reference osisRef="Jer.49.31">Jr 49:31</reference>.<div eID="gen23803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bashan--</hi>famed for its cattle (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">Psa 22:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Am 4:1</reference>). Parallel to this passage is <reference osisRef="Jer.50.19">Jr 50:19</reference>. Bashan and Gilead, east of Jordan, were chosen by Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh, as abounding in pastures suited for their many cattle (<reference osisRef="Num.32.1-Num.32.42">Nu 32:1-42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12-Deut.3.17">De 3:12-17</reference>). <div eID="gen23804" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ca2fbe4db2e564f99b2ed360bbe7fd6ed3ff7ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12813"/><div sID="gen23805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12813"/><hi type="bold">15. thy ... him--</hi>both referring to Israel. So in <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">Mi 7:19</reference> the person is changed from the first to the third, "us ... our ... their." Jehovah here answers Micah's prayer in <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">Mi 7:14</reference>, assuring him, that as He delivered His people from Egypt by miraculous power, so He would again "show" it in their behalf (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jr 16:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen23805" type="x-p"/>
entries.5269dd9030aabede90a177792ad73883f466fe12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12814"/><div sID="gen23806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12814"/><hi type="bold">16. shall see--</hi>the "marvellous things" (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.15">Mi 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Is 26:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confounded at all their might--</hi>having so suddenly proved unavailing: that might wherewith they had thought that there is nothing which they could not effect against God's people.<div eID="gen23807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay ... hand upon ... mouth--</hi>the gesture of silence (<reference osisRef="Job.21.5">Job 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.4">40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Is 52:15</reference>). They shall be struck dumb at Israel's marvellous deliverance, and no longer boast that God's people is destroyed.<div eID="gen23808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ears ... deaf--</hi>They shall stand astounded so as not to hear what shall be said [Grotius]. Once they had eagerly drunk in all rumors as so many messages of victories; but then they shall be afraid of hearing them, because they continually fear new disasters, when they see the God of Israel to be so powerful [Calvin]. They shall close their ears so as not to be compelled to hear of Israel's successes. <div eID="gen23809" type="x-p"/>
entries.f808ed148971f6fccd92ad73923e586f5cc90a12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12815"/><div sID="gen23810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12815"/><hi type="bold">17. lick the dust--</hi>in abject prostration as suppliants (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.9">Psa 72:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Is 49:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">65:25</reference>).<div eID="gen23810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">move out of their holes--</hi>As reptiles from their holes, they shall come forth from their hiding-places, or fortresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.45">Psa 18:45</reference>), to give themselves up to the conquerors. More literally, "they shall tremble from," that is, tremblingly come forth from their coverts.<div eID="gen23811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like worms--</hi>reptiles or crawlers (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.24">De 32:24</reference>).<div eID="gen23812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall be afraid of the Lord--</hi>or, they shall in fear turn with haste to the Lord. Thus the antithesis is brought out. They shall tremble forth from their holes: they shall in trepidation turn to the Lord for salvation (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">Jr 33:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear because of thee--</hi>shall fear Thee, Jehovah (and so fear Israel as under Thy guardianship). There is a change here from speaking of God to speaking to God [Maurer]. Or rather, "shall fear thee, Israel" [Henderson]. <div eID="gen23814" type="x-p"/>
entries.42522250663537d796bdf41ecf5e2382b299a779: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12816"/><div sID="gen23815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12816"/>18. Grateful at such unlooked-for grace being promised to Israel, Micah breaks forth into praises of Jehovah.<div eID="gen23815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passeth by the transgression--</hi>not conniving at it, but forgiving it; leaving it unpunished, as a traveller passes by what he chooses not to look into (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.11">Pr 19:11</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">Am 7:8</reference>, and "mark iniquities," <reference osisRef="Ps.130.3">Psa 130:3</reference>.<div eID="gen23816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the remnant--</hi>who shall be permitted to survive the previous judgment: the elect remnant of grace (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.7">Mi 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.3">5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">7, 8</reference>).<div eID="gen23817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">retaineth not ... anger--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delighteth in mercy--</hi>God's forgiving is founded on His nature, which delights in loving-kindness, and is averse from wrath. <div eID="gen23819" type="x-p"/>
entries.a686119e0ec544c963717d720d060ff7c834674e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12817"/><div sID="gen23820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12817"/><hi type="bold">19. turn again--</hi>to us, from having been turned away from us.<div eID="gen23820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">subdue our iniquities--</hi>literally, "tread under foot," as being hostile and deadly to us. Without subjugation of our bad propensities, even pardon could not give us peace. When God takes away the guilt of sin that it may not condemn us, He takes away also the power of sin that it may not rule us.<div eID="gen23821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast ... into ... depths of the sea--</hi>never to rise again to view, buried out of sight in eternal oblivion: not merely at the shore side, where they may rise again.<div eID="gen23822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our ... their--</hi>change of person. Micah in the first case identifying himself and his sins with his people and their sins; in the second, speaking of them and their sins. <div eID="gen23823" type="x-p"/>
entries.e37f09023eedc5e11b0b7559e155f2e1295326ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12818"/><div sID="gen23824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12818"/><hi type="bold">20. perform the truth--</hi>the faithful promise.<div eID="gen23824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Jacob ... Abraham--</hi>Thou shalt make good to their posterity the promise made to the patriarchs. God's promises are called "mercy," because they flow slowly from grace; "truth," because they will be surely performed (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.72">Lu 1:72</reference>, 73; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.24">1Th 5:24</reference>).<div eID="gen23825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sworn unto our fathers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.105.9">Psa 105:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.10">10</reference>). The promise to Abraham is in <reference osisRef="Gen.12.2">Ge 12:2</reference>; to Isaac, in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.24">Ge 26:24</reference>; to Jacob, in <reference osisRef="Gen.28.13">Ge 28:13</reference>. This unchangeable promise implied an engagement that the seed of the patriarchs should never perish, and should be restored to their inheritance as often as they turned wholly to God (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1">De 30:1</reference>, 2). <chapter eID="Mic.7"/><div eID="gen23826" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen23519" osisID="Mic" type="book"/>

entries.a4423ff29c0a2ac54b6dd29c203b452ea1feb8a4: <div eID="gen34893" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34894" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34895" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34895" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34894" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34896" type="x-p"/> The prophet begins this chapter with lamenting the decay of piety and the growth of ungodliness, using a beautiful allegory to imply (as explained in <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mic 7:2</reference>) that the good man is as seldom to be met with as the early fig of best quality in the advanced season, or the cluster after the vintage, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.1">Mic 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mic 7:2</reference>. He then reproves and threatens in terms so expressive of great calamities as to be applied in the New Testament to times of the hottest persecution, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.3-Mic.7.6">Mic 7:3-6</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Mat.10.35">Mat 10:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.36">Mat 10:36</reference>. Notwithstanding which a Jew is immediately introduced declaring, in the name of his captive people, the strongest faith in the mercy of God the most submissive resignation to his will, and the firmest hope in his favor in future times, when they should triumph over their enemies, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.7-Mic.7.10">Mic 7:7-10</reference>. The prophet upon this resumes the discourse, and predicts their great prosperity and increase, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.11">Mic 7:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.12">Mic 7:12</reference>; although the whole land of Israel must first be desolated on account of the great wickedness of its inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.13">Mic 7:13</reference>. The prophet intercedes in behalf of his people, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">Mic 7:14</reference>. After which God is introduced promising, in very ample terms, their future restoration and prosperity, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.15-Mic.7.17">Mic 7:15-17</reference>. And then, to conclude, a chorus of Jews is introduced, singing a beautiful hymn of thanksgiving, suggested by the gracious promises which precede, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18-Mic.7.20">Mic 7:18-20</reference>. <div eID="gen34896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34897" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34898" type="x-p"/> Wo is me! - This is a continuation of the preceding discourse. And here the prophet points out the small number of the upright to be found in the land. He himself seemed to be the only person who was on God's side; and he considers himself as a solitary grape, which had escaped the general gathering. The word קץ kayits, which is sometimes used for summer, and summer fruits in general, is here translated late figs; and may here, says Bishop Newcome, be opposed to the early ripe fig of superior quality. See on <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">Hos 9:10</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Amo.8.1">Amo 8:1</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Amo.8.2">Amo 8:2</reference> (note). He desired to see the first-ripe fruit - distinguished and eminent piety; but he found nothing but a very imperfect or spurious kind of godliness.
entries.63e627675795cd7e097fac542a265f8450d9be48: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34899" type="x-p"/> The good man is perished out of the earth - A similar sentiment may be found, <reference osisRef="Psa.12.1">Psa 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa 57:1</reference>. As the early fig of excellent flavor cannot be found in the advanced season of summer, or a choice cluster of grapes after vintage, so neither can the good and upright man be discovered by searching in Israel. This comparison, says Bp. Newcome, is beautifully implied. <div eID="gen34899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34900" type="x-p"/> They hunt every man his brother with a net - This appears to be an allusion to the ancient mode of duel between the retiarius and secutor. The former had a casting net, which he endeavoured to throw over the head of his antagonist, that he might then despatch him with his short sword. The other parried the cast; and when the retiarius missed, he was obliged to run about the field to get time to set his net in right order for another throw. While he ran, the other followed, that he might despatch him before he should be able to recover the proper position of his net; and hence the latter was called secutor, the pursuer, as the other was called retiarius, or the net man. I have explained this before on Job, and other places; but because it is rarely noticed by commentators, I explain the allusion here once more. Abp. Newcome by not attending to this, has translated איש את אחיהו יצודו חרם ish eth achihu yatsudu cherem, "They hunt every man his brother for his destruction;" though he put net in the margin.
entries.b9042f8ab9ec1a6de115fef4f7d7038e920e01aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34901" type="x-p"/> That they may do evil with both hands - That is, earnestly, greedily, to the uttermost of their power. The Vulgate translates: Malum manuum suarum dicunt bonum; "The evil of their hands they call good." <div eID="gen34901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34902" type="x-p"/> The prince asketh - A bribe, to forward claims in his court. <div eID="gen34902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34903" type="x-p"/> The judge asketh for a reward - That he may decide the cause in favor of him who gives most money, whether the cause be good or evil. This was notoriously the case in our own country before the giving of Magna Charta; and hence that provision, Nulli vendemus justitiam aut rectum: "We will not sell justice to any man." And this was not the only country in which justice and judgment were put to sale. <div eID="gen34903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34904" type="x-p"/> The great man, he uttereth his mischievous desire - Such consider themselves above law, and they make no secret of their unjust determinations. And so they wrap it up - they all conjoin in doing evil in their several offices, and oppressing the poor; so our translators have interpreted the original ויעבתוה vayeabtuha, which the versions translate variously. Newcome has, "And they do abominably."
entries.28b74a0da7f0b4f6b11da5eae3308db232d7065a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34905" type="x-p"/> The best of them is as a brier - They are useless in themselves, and cannot be touched without wounding him that comes in contact with them. He alludes to the thick thorn hedges, still frequent in Palestine. <div eID="gen34905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34906" type="x-p"/> The day of thy watchmen - The day of vengeance, which the prophets have foreseen and proclaimed, is at hand. Now shall be their perplexity; no more wrapping up, all shall be unfolded. In that day every man will wish that he were different from what he is found to be; but he shall be judged for what he is, and for the deeds he has done.
entries.16833298c89e8cea6c3a96bcc2ff296e4ca76862: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34907" type="x-p"/> Trust ye not in a friend - These times will be so evil, and the people so wicked, that all bonds will be dissolved; and even the most intimate will betray each other, when they can hope to serve themselves by it. <div eID="gen34907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34908" type="x-p"/> On this passage, in the year 1798, I find I have written as follows: - "Trust ye not in a friend. - Several of those whom I have delighted to call by that name have deceived me. "Put ye not confidence in a guide. - Had I followed some of these I should have gone to perdition. "Keep the door of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. - My wife alone never deceived me." <div eID="gen34908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34909" type="x-p"/> It is now twenty-seven years since, and I find no cause to alter what I then wrote.
entries.f42d30cea774c53441f78a3345d25e75144eb840: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34910" type="x-p"/> For the son dishonoreth the father - See the use our Lord has made of these words, where he quotes them, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.21">Mat 10:21</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Mat.10.25">Mat 10:25</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Mat.10.36">Mat 10:36</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.eccaa009c6cacfc35a1b8237c36164667cf2388e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34911" type="x-p"/> Therefore I will look unto the Lord - Because things are so, I will trust in the Lord more firmly, wait for him more patiently, and more confidently expect to be supported, defended, and saved.
entries.420241465a9ecff7a5939b7105cb8062b5febd3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34912" type="x-p"/> Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy - The captive Israelites are introduced as speaking here and in the preceding verse. The enemy are the Assyrians and Chaldeans; the fall is their idolatry and consequent captivity; the darkness, the calamities they suffered in that captivity; their rise and light, their restoration and consequent blessedness. <div eID="gen34912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34913" type="x-p"/> To rejoice over the fall or miseries of any man, betrays a malignant spirit. I have known several instances where people professing to hold a very pure and Christian creed, having become unfaithful and fallen into sin, their opponents, who held a very impure and unchristian creed, have exulted with "Ha, ha! so would we have it!" and have shown their malignity more fully, by giving all possible publicity and circulation to such accounts. Perhaps in the sight of God this was worse than the poor wretch's fall, in which they exulted as having taken place in one who held a creed different from their own. But these arose again from their fall, while those jesters at holiness continued in the gall of bitterness and bonds of inward corruption.
